title: Astronomical Julian Date Clock
intro: Julian Date (JD) is a continuous count of days and fractions of a day. Astronomers use it to compare observations without month or year boundaries.
structure: The integer part advances at UTC noon, not midnight. The fraction is a decimal portion of a 24-hour model day. Three displayed fractional digits resolve 86.4 ordinary seconds; five resolve 0.864 seconds.
example: At 00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970 the reading is JD 2440587.500; at noon it is JD 2440588.000. At 12:00 UTC on 1 January 2000 it is JD 2451545.000. The higher-precision mode displays five fractional digits.
history: The Julian day-number convention is an astronomical chronological coordinate, not the Julian civil calendar.
model: Split Unix microseconds into floor-divided days and a nonnegative phase. Add the epoch day 2440587, advance the integer day when UTC phase reaches noon, and shift the fractional phase by half a day modulo one day. Floor the fraction at 1000 or 100000 ticks per day. Format the signed scaled value and schedule the next exact tick with upward millisecond rounding.
limits: The provider uses a Unix-based UTC-like uniform day coordinate, not a UT1, TT or TDB ephemeris conversion or leap-second table. Civil offset and geographical coordinates do not affect it. JD and MJD have distinct epoch and rollover conventions.
